opener.title: Mental Health Hospital
opener.tags: Healthcare · Federation · Clash detection · Issue management · CDE
opener.overview: A single storey mental health unit with a basement, walkway and plant roof in New South Wales, supplied as a training dataset of seven discipline models. I took the set from unloaded links with broken paths to an ISO 19650 named federation, ran a ten test clash matrix over four runs, and closed with 94 owned issues, two RFIs to the engineers, a BCF package, a coordinated services sheet and a shared package in Autodesk Construction Cloud.
facts: Revit 2027 · Navisworks Manage 2027 · Autodesk Construction Cloud · Excel · BCF 2.1
New South Wales, Australia. Training dataset, not a live commission.
BIM coordinator: model setup and naming, federation, clash matrix, triage, issue log, RFIs, CDE workflow

items.h1: Federation of seven discipline models under ISO 19650 naming
items.herocap: discipline models federated on one origin into MHH-MEJ-ZZ-ZZ-M3-Z-0001.nwf

qs.title: What was wrong
qs.p: The dataset arrived as a workshared architectural host with seven unloaded links, each pointing at an absolute path on someone else's computer, under course file names that said nothing about discipline or status.

qs.title: What I decided
qs.p: Work on copies and never overwrite received information. Each model was saved as a compacted copy under an ISO 19650 container name with role codes A, S, M, E, F and P, and every link was repointed. Before federating I checked placement: all links sit at the host origin with zero rotation, and Basement 64.90, Ground 70.00, Ceiling 72.70, Walkway 73.40 and Roof 77.00 match in every model.

qs.title: What changed
qs.p: Seven NWC caches named to the same convention, so every object in Navisworks traces back to its Revit source. The first pass came out light: the electrical cache was 0.2 MB with 1,374 light fittings in the model, because the export view had 30 categories switched off. Caught, fixed and re-exported before any clash test ran.

qs.title: What I would do next
qs.p: Move the set to shared coordinates from the survey point before it leaves the training environment. Origin to origin only holds while every author starts at the same point.

items.h1: Ten clash tests set by discipline pair and services precedence
items.herocap: raw clashes from Run 1, before any triage

qs.title: What was wrong
qs.p: A catch all MEP v MEP test floods results with duplicates and gives every clash two possible owners, so nobody acts.

qs.title: What I decided
qs.p: One discipline pair per test, so each clash lands with one owner. Precedence runs structure first, then gravity drainage because falls fix its route, then large ductwork, pressure pipework, sprinklers and finally containment. Tolerance follows the trade: 25 mm for duct against steel, 15 mm for pipework, 10 mm at the ceiling, and a 50 mm clearance test for trays near water. Light fittings were left out of the ceiling test because recessed lights sit in the ceiling by design.

qs.title: What changed
qs.p: Run 1 returned 1,123 clashes, and 836 of them (75 percent) sat in the three structure tests. That pattern pointed at the selection sets rather than the design, which the next page unpicks. A zero in T05 was tested before it was trusted: temporary copies at 0 mm hard and 50 mm clearance returned 0 and 1, so the zero is real.

qs.title: What I would do next
qs.p: T10, structure against trays, was added after the Run 2 review exposed a gap. On the next project it goes into the matrix from day one.

items.h1: Removal of false clashes from the first clash run
items.herocap: raw clashes in Run 1, live clashes after the selection sets were rebuilt

qs.title: What was wrong
qs.p: 75 percent of Run 1 sat in the structure tests, and T02 alone reported 539. Numbers that lopsided usually mean the selection is wrong, not the design.

qs.title: What I decided
qs.p: Interrogate the results by category before touching any geometry. The whole file sets for structure, drainage and sprinklers had pulled in Revit room volumes (119 clashes in T02 and 119 in T03), 361 slab sleeves and 76 wall penetrations designed to sit inside the slab, plus analytical panels, topography and masses. Not one sprinkler clashed with structure. I rebuilt STR, DRAIN and SPRK to physical categories only and kept the originals as WholeFile_Run1 sets for the audit trail. Nothing was hidden or approved to make the number fall.

qs.title: What changed
qs.p: T02 fell from 539 to 1, T03 from 154 to 0 and T04 from 17 to 0. Run 2 held 370 live clashes, grouped into 138 issues: an 88 percent reduction from Run 1, with every removal explained.

qs.title: What I would do next
qs.p: Make the physical category rule part of the search set template, so the next federation starts at Run 2 quality.

items.h1: 121 duct clashes classified into four issue types with owners
items.herocap: T01 structure v duct clashes, split into owner classes

qs.title: What was wrong
qs.p: T01 looked like one problem, ducts through beams. Sent that way, all 121 would have gone to the structural engineer, who would have returned most of them.

qs.title: What I decided
qs.p: Break T01 down by steel member, duct size and system. Roof and deck openings are intentional, so the architect confirms upstands. A duct deeper than its beam cannot pass through it, so mechanical drops or reroutes. Bracing and posts cannot be penetrated. Only ten small ducts, under roughly 60 percent of beam depth, went to structural as web opening candidates, with that rule of thumb stated and the real limit left to the engineer.

qs.title: What changed
qs.p: Structural receives 10 clashes in RFI 001 instead of 121. RFI 002 asks the electrical engineer to choose a tray route through the ceiling void, settling 69 linked issues with one answer. The single T02 clash turned out to be a sanitary riser fitting 20 mm into a 100 mm slab: an alignment fix for the drainage modeller, not a structural question.

qs.title: What I would do next
qs.p: When RFI 001 returns opening sizes, model the openings in the structural model and rerun T01 to confirm all ten close.

items.herocap: clashes cleared and created by the Run 3 tray lift

qs.title: What was wrong
qs.p: In Run 3 the electrical trays were lifted 150 to 250 mm to clear the ceiling zone, and T08 fell by 78. Checked against T08 alone, it looked like a fix.

qs.title: What I decided
qs.p: Every geometric change is rerun against the whole matrix before it is accepted. The rerun showed 78 trays driven into steel beams in T10, up to 477 mm deep, and 26 into ductwork in T07. The void between ceiling and beam soffit cannot hold the trays at their width and route, so it is a design decision for the electrical engineer, not a modeller's move. I restored the Run 2 electrical model, checked byte for byte with cmp, re-exported and raised RFI 002.

qs.title: What changed
qs.p: Run 4 matched the Run 2 baseline on every test, 430 live clashes, with the lifted model archived for the record. Reporting went out as a custom HTML report with one card per issue group, an issue log with live summary formulas, a BCF 2.1 package of 94 topics (284 XML files, all parsing cleanly) and a coordinated services sheet framing both RFI zones.

qs.title: What I would do next
qs.p: A services zone study drawn as sections (ceiling level, beam soffit, duct zone) before any tray moves again.

items.h1: ISO 19650 workflow in Autodesk Construction Cloud
items.herocap: ISO 19650 information states in Autodesk Construction Cloud, captured 23 Nov 2026

qs.title: What was wrong
qs.p: Coordination files on one laptop have no status, no permissions and no audit trail. ISO 19650 expects a common data environment where information moves through WIP, Shared and Published states.

qs.title: What I decided
qs.p: Move the models to the cloud with Collaborate in the cloud, into discipline WIP folders. Apply the ISO 19650 naming template, set folder permissions so each team can only create in its own WIP folder, then let Design Collaboration discover the folders as teams and set up a coordination space with clash detection on.

qs.title: What changed
qs.p: Architectural, Mechanical and Structural run as teams. The architectural model was published as package Architectural (1), for consumption, and shared with every team. The timeline records the exchange, and the Shared folder now holds version 1 of the architectural model.

qs.title: What I would do next
qs.p: Add a one step review and approval so a shared package can move to Published with an A suitability code, and raise the RFI items as ACC Issues pinned to the model.

opener.title: Aussi Close
opener.tags: Residential · UK ISO 19650 sheets · Rooms and schedules · Families · Stair and attic
opener.overview: A three storey detached house in the UK for client Barr Paul Edeh: open plan living on the ground floor, three bedroom suites on the first, and a guest suite, family lounge and studio in the attic under three dormers. I designed the shell and the main floors. This stage took the model from bare walls to an issued P01 set in UK ISO 19650 style, with 43 rooms, a rebuilt loft stair, three families of my own and 16 sheets.

United Kingdom. Private residential scheme, portfolio issue S2.
Designer and BIM technician: rooms and areas, attic design, stair, families, schedules, sheet set

items.h1: Room data and schedule of accommodation
items.herocap: rooms, numbered by floor, 718 m² in total

qs.title: What was wrong
qs.p: The model held walls and little else: no rooms, one sample sheet, a level named Rool, default view names and 18 warnings. A house without rooms cannot be tagged, scheduled or checked.

qs.title: What I decided
qs.p: Number rooms by floor, 01.xx to 03.xx, from my written layout, and give each a Use value so the schedule groups living, sleeping, sanitary, service and circulation. The attic rooms sit under a slope, so the room computation height went to 1.2 m; at the default the sloped rooms do not enclose.

qs.title: What changed
qs.p: 43 rooms with tags on every plan. A double run of the room script made 28 zero area duplicates. I deleted them and wrote every later script to be safe to rerun.

items.h1: 16 sheet P01 issue to BS EN ISO 19650
items.herocap: sheets, each with a container name, a status and a revision that agree

qs.title: What was wrong
qs.p: One sample sheet with a sample revision on the cover. A set that is meant to read like a real issue needs every sheet to carry a number, a status and a revision that match the register.

qs.title: What I decided
qs.p: Name every sheet to BS EN ISO 19650 with the UK National Annex fields, and number by drawing type so the register sorts itself. One Mejarc A1 title block carries S2, SHARED and Portfolio issue at revision P01. View templates fix plans at 1:50, elevations at 1:100 and sections at 1:50, with crops and datum extents set per view.

qs.title: What changed
qs.p: 16 sheets at P01. Five came in a second pass: the foundation plan, three reflected ceiling plans and a 3D perspectives sheet. Their viewports first landed off the sheet because the ceiling plans picked up distant site lines; cropping each to its floor plan's crop fixed it.

qs.title: What I would do next
qs.p: Fix the dates. The title block date field prints 11/23/26 while the revision table on the same sheet says 23/11/2026, and the cover still shows 01/03/26. A UK reader sees a 23rd month. The next issue uses one format, ISO 8601, on every sheet.

items.h1: Loft stair, gable wall and ceiling coordination
items.herocap: minimum headroom over the rebuilt loft stair, against 2.0 m in Approved Document K

qs.title: What was wrong
qs.p: The loft stair arrived against the dormer cheek with no top landing. The gables had no inner leaf above 7050: the external wall type is vertically compound and its blockwork stops just under the attic floor, so the attic walls cleaned back to a face that did not exist and left a 110 mm strip. Nobody had drawn a ceiling or a way into the roof void.

qs.title: What I decided
qs.p: Check before moving anything. Rays cast up from every tread showed the headroom was fine and the landing was the problem, so the flight was rebuilt instead of rerouted: 20 risers at 180 mm, a 250 mm going and winders round a small newel. The gables got a 110 mm inner leaf type from 7050 to the roof. Editing the wall type's layers would be cleaner, but it changes every wall of that type, so I held it back.

qs.title: What changed
qs.p: A 965 mm top landing with a 900 mm guard on the well, gables with a real inner leaf, a flat collar ceiling at 2.7 m with the dormers vaulted, and a 600 by 700 loft hatch into the void. Sections CC and DD document each one.

qs.title: What I would do next
qs.p: Close what is still open. The FD20 door to the stair enclosure was lost in a later edit, the foyer and landing need a fire screen or sprinklers to complete the protected route, and the W trusses must become attic trusses or a cut roof.

items.h1: Parametric families for wardrobes, WCs and the loft hatch
items.herocap: parametric families built for this house: fitted wardrobe, close coupled WC, loft hatch

qs.title: What was wrong
qs.p: No residential WC, shower or fitted wardrobe family existed on the machine, so the first issue went out with empty WCs and loose shelving drawn in the walk in closets.

qs.title: What I decided
qs.p: Build them small and parametric. The wardrobe is Casework, with width, depth and height driven by aligned reference planes. The WC is a 400 by 660 close coupled pan. The hatch is a lining and panel set in an opening cut in the collar ceiling. Every instance carries a Comments code, MEJ_FF_03 or MEJ_FF_04, so it can be filtered and scheduled.

qs.title: What changed
qs.p: Six wardrobes replaced the shelving in four walk in closets. Side units in closets 2 and 3 were dropped because a 600 deep unit on that wall blocks the door. Five WCs went in, with Bathrooms 2 and 3 back to back on one soil stack.

qs.title: What I would do next
qs.p: Add a shower tray family so the guest shower room stops borrowing a bath, and set subcategories on all three families so they print at the right line weight.

opener.title: Aqualand Office Building
opener.tags: Commercial office · Uniclass 2015 · Schedules · IFC4 Reference View · Model health
opener.overview: A four storey office building with a lower ground plant level and roof plant in Austral, New South Wales. I modelled the geometry earlier; this project is about the information inside it. The rooms started with no departments and fifteen wrong names, and the IFC wrote every space as NOTDEFINED. It ends with all 62 rooms classified to Uniclass 2015, schedules on an ISO named sheet, an IFC4 file that passes both a schema check and a property check, and 48 fewer warnings.
facts: Austral, New South Wales, Australia. Portfolio model, not a live commission.
Designer and information manager: room data, classification, schedules, IFC export and validation, warnings, title block

items.herocap: rooms with a Department and a Uniclass SL code, out of 62

qs.title: What was wrong
qs.p: The room schedule held numbers and nothing else. No room had a department, 15 were named Room or misspelt, the project was still called NSW Office Building with number MEJ-001, and no door type carried a classification.

qs.title: What I decided
qs.p: Four shared parameters in a Classification group: Uniclass SL number and description on rooms, Pr number and description on door types. Rooms renumbered by level, LG.01 to RF.01, renamed and given a department from an agreed table, each matched on its old number and checked against its area before writing. Where Uniclass has no answer I chose and logged one: the verandah takes SL_90_20_91 Terraces, and male and female WCs share SL_35_80_89 because Uniclass does not split by gender.

qs.title: What changed
qs.p: The data now drives the drawings: a department colour scheme fills every room on six plans at 1:200.

items.h1: IFC4 export validated for schema and property content
items.herocap: IfcSpaces carrying a Uniclass reference, a Department and a base quantity area

qs.title: What was wrong
qs.p: In BIMcollab Zoom, space 03.10 read NOTDEFINED for both Predefined Type and Type Name. No room had an IFC Predefined Type, so Revit wrote one NOTDEFINED space type for all 62. The same check found IfcBuilding still named NSW Office Building, and CSI Uniformat riding along from Assembly Codes on 37 family types.

qs.title: What I decided
qs.p: IFC4 Reference View with base quantities, common property sets, shared coordinates and Uniclass 2015 as the only classification. IFC Predefined Type set on every room from IfcSpaceTypeEnum: 59 INTERNAL and 3 verandahs EXTERNAL, with a new IsExternal parameter so Pset_SpaceCommon reads True on the verandahs. Assembly Codes cleared, building name and address corrected.

qs.title: What changed
qs.p: Zero schema errors and zero EXPRESS rule violations in IfcOpenShell. Space 03.10 now reads INTERNAL, same GUID, same Uniclass code. Every count reconciled with Revit.

qs.title: What I caught
qs.p: The first scripted export used the new parameter mapping. It dropped every property set, leaving Department and area on 0 of 62 spaces, and it still validated with 0 errors. I rejected it and exported again with the classic mapping. A clean schema report proves the file is well formed, nothing more.

items.h1: Warning reduction and ISO 19650 title block
items.herocap: warnings, with every room area checked before and after

qs.title: What was wrong
qs.p: 133 warnings, 119 of them wall and room separation line overlaps. Section AA showed 130 cyan separation lines and level heads printing on top of each other. The schedule sheet sat on the Autodesk sample title block, with its logo and four empty ISO boxes.

qs.title: What I decided
qs.p: Delete only the 48 separation lines lying on room bounding walls, behind a guard: compare every room area before and after, roll back if any changed by more than 0.05 m² or hit zero. A trial on the other 71 zeroed 36 rooms, so it was rolled back and those lines stay. For the sheet, a Mejarc title block whose ISO labels bind to the shared parameters already in the family.

qs.title: What changed
qs.p: 85 warnings. The largest area change was room 00.02, 64.985 to 64.959 m². The section now reads cleanly, and the sheet carries S2, SHARED, Portfolio issue and revision P01 on a numbering sequence called MEJ Preliminary P.

qs.title: What I would do next
qs.p: Decide the last 71 overlaps wall by wall, then purge the old sample title block. The title block date prints 11/22/26; the next issue uses ISO 8601.

opener.overview: A five storey civic office building with a curved glazed front, an entrance plinth and a car park, first drawn as a learning model for a site in Uganda and documented here against a notional UK client. The model was rich in geometry and poor in information: 56 warnings, 521 unused elements, four floor plan DWGs embedded as imports, placeholder project information and no sheets in use. I made it fit to share under ISO 19650, then wrote down the rules that keep it that way.

items.h1: Audit and cleanup of an inherited model
items.herocap: unused elements purged in three passes: 494, then 60, then 55

qs.title: What was wrong
qs.p: The model held 327 walls and 139 doors but no rooms, two empty sheets with no title block, four floor plan DWGs imported instead of linked, and project information that still read Project Number and Enter address here. A team receiving it would spend its first day cleaning.

qs.title: What I decided
qs.p: Work on a copy named to the container convention and leave the original untouched. Delete the imported DWGs instead of converting them to links: imports carry their own layers and line styles into the model and can never be updated. Purge until nothing is left, because removing a family frees its materials and patterns for the next pass. Keep the title block type and all 13 view templates for the sheet work.

qs.title: What changed
qs.p: Every change ran as a named Revit transaction, so each step sits separately in the Undo history.

items.h1: Warnings reduced from 56 to 7 with documented exceptions
items.herocap: warnings, cut by 87 percent without moving a wall

qs.title: What was wrong
qs.p: 56 warnings. 32 came from quad corner mullions at curtain wall ends that join nothing. 11 walls were attached to the pent slab while their tops were already set by level and offset, so the attachment pointed at a slab they never touched. Three stepped slabs overlapped the ground slab.

qs.title: What I decided
qs.p: Fix the relationship before the geometry. Detach the walls, which moves nothing. Make a rectangular mullion with the same 150 by 150 section and swap the 32 corners to it. The stepped slabs looked like errors, so I confirmed the design intent before touching them: they are entrance plinths at 0, minus 150 and minus 270, so they stay and get joined, plinth cutting. For each duplicate wall I checked what it hosted and kept the one carrying the door.

qs.title: What changed
qs.p: 56 to 13 after the walls and mullions, 9 after the plinth joins, 7 after the duplicates. The joins also stop a quantity takeoff counting the overlapping concrete twice.

qs.title: What I would do next
qs.p: Rebuild the 15 in place casework families as loadable families so they can be scheduled and reused. They are the last thing in this model a second team would curse.

items.html:
Why keep seven

Zero was reachable by deleting things that mattered. Straightening an off axis wall drags every joined wall with it, and changing the ramp changes its gradient, which is a design decision. A justified residue is what a BIM manager wants to read. A clean zero usually hides a deletion.

Interview story

The plinth slabs. Asking before changing geometry, and knowing the overlap would have overstated the concrete.

items.h1: Project information, BEP extract and document register
items.herocap: placeholder fields in Project Information, replaced by ISO 19650 codes

qs.title: What was wrong
qs.p: Project information held placeholders: Project Number, Enter address here, Project Status. Nothing in the file said who made it, what state it was in, or what it was called, so every title block and IFC export would have carried blanks.

qs.title: What I decided
qs.p: ISO 19650 sets the codes, not the Revit fields, so I put each code where Revit can pass it on: originator MEJ in Organization, City Council Offices as the building name for IfcBuilding, S0 as the status, PRJC as the project code. Then a BEP extract covering naming, status and revision codes, CDE gates, level of information need and the checks a model passes before it is shared.

qs.title: What changed
qs.p: A register of four containers. The model sits at P01.02 because P01.01 was the state I received; it becomes P01 when shared.

qs.title: What I would do next
qs.p: Two loose ends before the register goes out. The project number still read PRJC 001 at the audit, and codes carry no spaces. Sheet A101 Unnamed holds no views and needs a purpose or deleting.
